newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: U.S. businesses urge ASEAN to open investment door.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businesses urge ASEAN to open investment door.

text.p: Some of the biggest names in U.S. business on Tuesday urged Malaysia and other booming economies in Southeast Asia to open up to foreign investment or be left behind in fierce competition for international capital.

United Technologies chief executive officer George David, heading the nearly 100-member U.S.-ASEAN Business Council delegation, said countries in the region relied too much on trade for growth and not enough on investment.

ASEAN exports $250 billion a year or about 40 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), he told reporters in Kuala Lumpur. Imports currently run around $300 billion a year or about 50 percent of GDP.
"An unusually high percentage of GDP is tied up in exports and imports," he said. In Europe trade accounted for 8-9 percent of GDP and in the United States it was 7-8 percent, he said.
Foreign direct investment accounted for 2-3 percent of GDP in ASEAN -- in China it was five times that figure, he said.

"There's not going to be enough investment capital around...to fuel growth," former U.S. Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen told the news conference. "That competition for capital has to be understood in Southeast Asia."
Malaysia, in fact, has done well with foreign investment which has helped power the country into a decade of eight percent annual GDP growth or better.
Malaysia lured in nearly $40 billion in the 1990s, mostly in export-oriented manufacturing -- one of the highest foreign investment levels in the world.
In 1996, it nearly doubled to 17.1 billion ringgit ($6.9 billion) from 9.1 billion in 1995 ($3.6 billion).

David said the companies in his delegation were responsible for $20 billion in foreign investment in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), which groups Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Speaking to the group earlier, International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz said Malaysia was reviewing its policies as a result of various multilateral trade initiatives.
"All these new issues in themselves necessitate review and change in Malaysia's policies, particularly to allow industry to adapt quickly to regional and global dynamics," Rafidah said.
But she said the country remained opposed to opening up its financial services industry to more foreign investment, which the U.S.-ASEAN Business Council said it was keen to see.
Malaysia has for years frozen new licenses for foreign banks and will not allow the 16 already here to open new branches.

The council, whose members include Chrysler Corp, Caterpillar Inc, Motorola Inc, McDonald's Corp, Lockheed Martin Corp, Federal Express and Exxon among others, was to meet Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad later on Tuesday.
They would push "national treatment" for foreign investors, which meant allowing foreign companies to compete on the same terms and by the same rules as local ones, David said.

Mahathir has strongly opposed national treatment, which is part of a global multilateral investment agreement currently under negotiation. He says it is like telling pygmies to play against giants in a game where only the giants know the rules.
Laura D'Andrea Tyson, former Economic Advisor to President Bill Clinton and part of the delegation, said the argument has "intuitive appeal".
"But experience shows that the home team doesn't become better with that protection," although they do when exposed to the standards of international competition, she said.
